tagline.text: A private island with two sea caves, a stop on Boracay island-hopping tours

location.label: Location
location.text: Private island off Malay, Aklan, near Tambisaan Point southeast of Boracay

duration.label: Time needed
duration.text: 1–2 hours (one stop on an island-hopping tour)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱300~2,000 (based on an entrance fee of about ₱200~300 and a group island-hopping tour at around ₱1,700)

children.text: Crystal Cove Island is a small private island in the sea southeast of Boracay, known for two sea caves you can swim into, clear water, and a coastal trail. It is a day-visit spot with no overnight stays, usually visited as one stop on a Boracay island-hopping tour, and it charges its own entrance fee.
Crystal Cove Island is a small private island off Malay, Aklan. It is described as about
15–25 minutes

by boat from Boracay's main island, near Tambisaan Point. At roughly 2 hectares it is small enough to explore in a short time, and the island's owner charges an entrance fee and manages it. The "cove" in the name means a small bay or inlet, and here it refers to two cave inlets beneath the cliffs where the waves come and go. It is not a long beach for walking like White Beach on Boracay but a place to experience caves and sea in a short time, and thinking of it that way keeps expectations in line with reality.

The heart of the island is the two caves (coves) below the seaward cliff. According to older descriptions, Cove 1 is reached by a steep, slippery rock staircase, while Cove 2 is larger and entered via a concrete path and a low tunnel. The clear blue water inside the caves, where the waves flow in and out, is the main draw, and because so many people come to take photos, it is easy to combine snorkeling and photography.

The island has a coastal trail, wooden bridges, native-style huts, and picnic huts with tables, and you can snorkel in designated shallow areas. Visitors report that there is no electricity and that ATMs and card payments do not work, so bring cash and a power bank. Older reviews said the island can also be rented for weddings and events, but it does not offer overnight stays. Recent reviews often say the cave entrances and bridges get crowded from mid-morning, so if possible make it your first stop.

Most travelers do not come on their own but stop here on an island-hopping tour. A typical 3–5 hour course combines it with Crocodile Island (snorkeling), Magic Island (optional cliff jumping), Puka Beach, and similar stops. So it is more accurate to think of it as a place to swim in the caves during a hopping itinerary than as a destination to visit by itself. The island operator can change facilities and entrance policies, so be sure to ask whether the fee is included when you book a tour. The departure beach for hopping boats changes by season: a 2014 blog explains that during the southwest monsoon (habagat,
July–September
) boats leave from Bulabog Beach on the east side, and otherwise from White Beach. Check with your operator whether this is still the case.

Two caves, Cove 1 and Cove 2, sit below the cliff, and the water inside is clear and blue. Swimming and photographing the rock formations are the focus of a visit, and morning is said to have the best light. Cove 1 is reached by a steep rock staircase, so take care if you have weak knees or are with young children, while Cove 2 is relatively larger and approached by a flat path.

A marked loop trail passes cliff viewpoints, wooden bridges, and huts. The island is small, so even a slow walk does not take long, and photos looking down at the sea and toward Boracay come out well.

In designated shallow areas you can see tropical fish and corals. You can bring or rent gear, and some tour packages include it. Do not step on or touch the corals. Some reviews say boats crowd the other hopping snorkeling spot, Crocodile Island, so the shallow area at Crystal Cove can be a relatively quiet alternative.

Bamboo paths, bridges, huts, and the caves all make good backdrops, and many pre-wedding and content shoots take place here. Golden light around 4 PM is said to be good, but last entry is early, so check the hours.
The island has huts and tables where you can eat packed meals or snacks. Bringing your own food is said to be allowed, but rules can change, so check at the entrance.
Itineraries often combine it with Crocodile Island, Magic Island, and Puka Beach. One boat charter covers several places, so the travel burden is light.
Board the tour boat at your hotel pickup or meeting point. The departure beach is either on the White Beach side or the Bulabog side, depending on the season.
Snorkel near Crocodile Island.
Land at Crystal Cove, pay the entrance fee, and explore the two caves.
Walk the trail, take photos, and snorkel in the shallow area.
Have lunch on the boat or at a beach restaurant, then head back.
Tour order and stops differ by operator, and the order can change with sea conditions on the day. When you book, ask whether Crystal Cove can be your first stop.

items.title: Private boat route
items.subtitle: Go early to avoid the crowds

children.text: Book a boat so you arrive as soon as the island opens and enter early.
Swim in the caves and take photos while few people are there.
Move on to the other hopping stops.
Return to your hotel to rest, or move on to another beach such as Puka Beach.
Entry is generally said to start at 8 AM, but this can change at the operator's discretion. If you take a private boat that leaves early, time your arrival so you do not get there before opening.

items.title: From Manila to Caticlan or Kalibo

children.text: Flights run from Manila to Caticlan Airport (MPH), which is close to Boracay, or Kalibo International Airport (KLO). Airlines and routes change by season, so check when you book.
From Kalibo Airport to the Caticlan jetty port takes about
1.5–2 hours
by bus or van.
From Iloilo City, buses to Caticlan are reported to leave frequently from the Tagbak Terminal in Jaro from early morning through the afternoon and take about
5–6 hours
. From Roxas City or San Jose (Antique), go via Kalibo.
From the Caticlan jetty port, a public ferry takes about
10–20 minutes
to reach Cagban Jetty Port on Boracay (2026 guides say 10–15 minutes, earlier ones 15–20).
Then take a tricycle or e-trike to your hotel or the hopping departure point. Depending on the destination it takes about
5–30 minutes
(5–20 minutes from Cagban to hotels; some guides say 20–30 to farther departure beaches).
On Boracay, tricycles and electric three-wheelers are the main way to get around. Many hopping operators include hotel pickup, so ask when you book.
Crystal Cove is usually reached by hopping tour boat. It is about
10–25 minutes
by boat from the departure point.
The entrance fee is often not included in the tour. Ask whether it is included when you book.
The best time is the
November–May
dry season, when the sea is calm and the sky is clear. Some guides suggest late November to early December or late January to early February if you want fewer crowds.

In the rainy season, waves and weather are unstable, boats may be canceled, and entering the caves can be dangerous. Be especially careful in the caves right after rain or at high tide. Early morning is quiet and has good light. Hopping operators adjust or cancel tours in bad weather, so it is safer to leave a spare day in your schedule.

There is no accommodation on the island, so you stay on Boracay's main island. Hotels near the hopping departure beach, in Station 2 or on the Bulabog side, make for easy mornings, and hotels on the White Beach side have better nightlife. If you want an early start to hopping, a hotel near the departure beach is convenient in the morning, and if you plan to sleep in, you can put price and facilities ahead of location. Room rates vary widely by season, so check on a booking site. Environmental rules and fees on Boracay change often, so check the notices before you arrive.

Food on the island is limited, so use the lunch included in your tour package (on the boat or at a beach restaurant) or bring snacks and water. Visitors report that the island has no electricity and that ATMs and card payments do not work, so carry cash. After the tour it is usual to eat seafood near your hotel or rest, so do not pack your evening too tightly.
The entrance fee is often not included in the tour price, so check when you book and carry cash.
The cave floors are slippery. Aqua shoes or trekking sandals are safer than flip-flops.
Bring a towel, swimsuit, waterproof phone case, and dry bag.
There is no electricity, so bring a power bank.
Going early in the morning means fewer crowds and better light in the caves.
Use a sunscreen that does not harm corals when snorkeling.
Check that your tour operator and boat provide safety equipment such as life jackets.
Sharing a boat with others lowers the cost per person. Boracay is expensive, so renting a private boat alone is a heavy expense.
Carry enough cash for the entrance fee, snacks, and tips, but since you will not stay long on the island, leave valuables at your hotel and take only what you need in a waterproof pouch.
The caves can be dangerous at high tide or after rain. Follow the safety signs and staff instructions, and do not take risks on cliffs or slippery areas.

The island is private, so the operator sets and changes the fees, hours, and rules. Sources give different prices, so confirm locally. This information compares several travel sites and reviews from the past one to two years, and an official operator page could not be confirmed.
Hours are generally given as 8 AM–5 PM (last entry around 4 PM), but no confirmed official notice was found.
The island has restrooms, but few of them, so you may have to wait in peak season. Take your trash with you and do not touch marine life.
During the rainy and typhoon seasons, hopping can be canceled. Check the weather and boat operation notices.
Visitors report that ATMs and card payments do not work on the island, so prepare cash in advance.
In peak season there can be long lines on the entrance stairs and bridges, so move slowly and give way to others.
Boracay's main island,
Boracay
, is the hopping departure point and the center of any trip, with hotels, restaurants, and nightlife.
Puka Shell Beach
is a shell-strewn beach in the north of Boracay that is often included in the same hopping itinerary.
An island shaped like a crocodile, and the snorkeling stop visited most often. Check whether the tour includes its entrance fee.
An optional stop known for cliff jumping, with a separate entrance fee.
